name: Duomo di San Matteo
blurb: The Norman cathedral over the tomb of Saint Matthew the Evangelist, with an arcaded courtyard and a bell tower of the 12th century.
text: Robert Guiscard, the Norman who had just taken Salerno, built the cathedral from 1080, and Pope Gregory VII consecrated it in 1084. The pope died in exile in Salerno a year later and lies buried here. In the crypt, covered in baroque marble and frescoes, are the relics of Saint Matthew, brought to Salerno in 954.

You go in through a courtyard of arches on old Roman columns, lined with Roman sarcophagi, and through bronze doors cast in Constantinople. The bell tower beside it, with its round top, is the landmark of the old town.

name: Via dei Mercanti
blurb: The merchants’ street of the medieval town, a narrow lane of shops across the whole centro storico.
text: Via dei Mercanti runs through the old town from the Arco di Arechi to Piazza Sedile di Portanova, more or less where the main street of the Roman and Lombard town ran. Its shops have been here since the Middle Ages, when Salerno traded with the whole Mediterranean.
Narrow side lanes climb from it towards the Duomo and the hill, under arches and past small churches. In winter the Luci d’Artista hang their lights over it.

name: Lungomare Trieste
blurb: The seafront promenade under the palms, with the Gulf of Salerno in front and the Amalfi Coast on the horizon.
text: Between the town and the sea runs the Lungomare Trieste, a wide promenade lined with palms and gardens. On a clear day you see the whole gulf from here, from the cliffs of the Amalfi Coast in the west to the plain of Paestum in the south.
It is where Salerno comes out in the evening: for a walk, an ice cream or a seat on a bench looking at the sea.

name: Corso Vittorio Emanuele
blurb: Salerno’s long shopping street, closed to cars, from the old town to the station.
text: The Corso runs straight for about a kilometre from Piazza Sedile di Portanova, at the edge of the old town, to the railway station. It was laid out in the 19th century, when the town grew east beyond its medieval walls.
Closed to cars, it is lined with shops, cafés and palazzi, and in the evening the whole town walks up and down it for the passeggiata.

name: Teatro Verdi
blurb: The town’s opera house of 1872, a small copy of the San Carlo in Naples, red and gold inside.
text: The Teatro Verdi opened in 1872 beside the Villa Comunale. Inside it is a horseshoe of boxes in red and gold, built after the example of the Teatro San Carlo in Naples.
Its curtain, painted by Domenico Morelli, shows the people of Salerno driving out the Saracens. It still has an opera season every year.

name: Villa Comunale
blurb: The town’s 19th-century garden, shady and green, between the Teatro Verdi and the sea.
text: The Villa Comunale is Salerno’s public garden, laid out in the 19th century at the west end of the town, beside the Teatro Verdi and a few steps from the Lungomare.
Its paths run under tall trees past a fountain and busts of famous Salernitans: a cool place on a hot afternoon, and in winter the heart of the Luci d’Artista.

name: Giardino della Minerva
blurb: A garden of medicinal plants on terraces above the old town, among the oldest botanical gardens in Europe.
text: In the early 14th century the doctor Matteo Silvatico grew the plants for his medicines here, on terraces climbing the hill, to teach the students of the Scuola Medica Salernitana. It is held to be one of the first botanical gardens in Europe.
Restored and opened to the public in 2001, it again grows hundreds of medicinal plants, watered by old channels and fountains, with a pergola at the top and a view over the roofs to the sea.

name: Medieval aqueduct
local: Acquedotto medievale, the Ponti del Diavolo
blurb: The tall arches of the medieval aqueduct, which legend says the devil built in a single night.
text: Above Via Arce the high pointed arches of the old aqueduct still stand, which brought water to a monastery in the Middle Ages. People call them the Ponti del Diavolo, the Devil’s Bridges.
Legend says the alchemist Pietro Barliario built them in one night with the devil’s help. A lane of the old town still carries his name.

name: Stazione Marittima
blurb: Zaha Hadid’s ferry terminal on the Molo Manfredi, where the boats leave for Amalfi, Positano and Capri.
text: The ferry terminal on the Molo Manfredi, shaped like an oyster, is by the architect Zaha Hadid. It opened in 2016, a few weeks after her death.
From the quay beside it the boats leave for the Amalfi Coast, Positano and Capri: the most beautiful way to see the coast is from the sea.

name: Castello di Arechi
blurb: The castle on the hill above the town, strengthened by the Lombard prince Arechis II, with the whole gulf at its feet.
text: High on the hill behind the town stands the castle that Arechis II, the Lombard prince of Benevento, strengthened in the 8th century when he made Salerno his capital. Normans, Swabians and Aragonese all built on it after him.
Its walls and towers now hold a small museum, and from the top you see the whole Gulf of Salerno, from the Amalfi Coast to Paestum. It lies above the piece of the town in the game.

name: Scuola Medica Salernitana
blurb: The first medical school of medieval Europe, where women taught and practised medicine too.
text: From the 10th century doctors in Salerno taught medicine from Greek, Latin, Arabic and Jewish sources, and the town became known as the Hippocratic City. Women studied and taught there as well, the most famous of them Trotula, whose name a street of the old town still carries.

Its health rules in verse, the Regimen Sanitatis Salernitanum, were read all over Europe. The school was closed in 1811; its story is told in a small museum in the church of San Gregorio on Via dei Mercanti.

name: Luci d’Artista
blurb: Every winter artists light up the streets, squares and gardens of Salerno with huge installations of light.
text: Since 2006, from November to January, Salerno hangs works of light by artists over its streets and squares: whole galaxies, animals, gardens and fairy tales in lights, from the Villa Comunale to the Corso and the old town.
The Luci d’Artista have become one of the largest light festivals in Italy, and bring coach loads of visitors to the town every winter.

name: Sfogliatella
blurb: The shell of crisp layered pastry filled with ricotta and semolina, born in a convent on the Amalfi Coast.
text: The sfogliatella is a shell of thin, crisp layers of pastry, filled with ricotta, semolina and candied orange peel. Its ancestor, the Santa Rosa, was first made in the 17th century by the nuns of the convent of Santa Rosa in Conca dei Marini, on the Amalfi Coast just west of Salerno.
You eat it warm, with an espresso, in any café on the Corso.
